clue.text: Pushing driving seat that's faulty

indicators.note: something faulty is not working as built, so its letters are put back together another way

parts.note: the two words taken letter for letter as the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone complains that the driver's seat in their car is broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pushing' looks like a verb, but here it is the noun sense: the activity of promoting goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Promoting a product hard to buyers is commonly called pushing it, which is exactly what commercial publicity does.

clue.text: Some sauerkraut put up in cupboard

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting something up means it reads from bottom to top
only a part of the following word is wanted, a run of its letters

parts.note: the run of letters in the middle of the word

explanation.surface: Pickled cabbage is stored away on a kitchen shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit inside sauerKRAut and read upwards in the grid to spell ARK.
explanation.definitionFit: An ark is an old word for a chest or storage box, close enough to a cupboard for crossword use.

clue.text: Off to visit Virginia holiday home?

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone else's place, so one piece enters another

parts.note: the postal abbreviation for the US state
feeling off means unwell

explanation.surface: Someone is heading off to stay at a holiday house in Virginia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off' reads as departing, but it means unwell, as food that has gone off; VA is the US postal code for Virginia.
explanation.definitionFit: A villa is a large rented house in the sun, the classic place to stay on a summer break.

clue.text: Discovers the truth about New York street fights?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for seeing through someone's deception
second meaning: gang brawls, as in West Side Story

explanation.walkthrough: To be rumbled, in British slang, is to be found out.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both British informal for exposing a trick and American slang for organised fights between gangs.

clue.text: On set, Piers cut off abruptly when about to butt in

indicators.note: an abrupt cut takes away the very end, so the final letter goes
about can mean around in a jumble, so the letters are moved round

parts.note: the two words run together as written
the name without its last letter

explanation.surface: A TV presenter called Piers is cut short on set whenever he is about to interrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: Piers looks like a celebrity's name; it simply supplies letters, minus the S.
explanation.definitionFit: To interpose is to put oneself between others in a conversation, which is interrupting or butting in.

clue.text: Freeze last of bolognese in single container

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: one thing placed in another goes inside it

parts.note: a cup holds liquid

indicators.note: the last of something is its final letter only

parts.note: the final letter of the sauce

explanation.surface: Leftover pasta sauce is put in a tub for the freezer.
explanation.walkthrough: E goes inside CUP after the C, with I in front.
explanation.definitionFit: To freeze over is to become covered or blocked with frost, which is what icing up describes.

clue.text: They should be charged for toast

definitions.text: They should be charged for toast

parts.words: They should be charged for toast
parts.note: surface reading: things that ought to be billed for a slice of grilled bread
setter's reading: drinking vessels that should be filled before everyone raises them to celebrate

explanation.walkthrough: 'Charged' means filled up with drink, and a toast is a celebratory drink, not grilled bread.
explanation.definitionFit: Before a toast, guests are told to charge their drinking vessels, meaning fill them with wine.

clue.text: Embarrassing error follows Best's header for Marsh

indicators.note: whatever follows comes after, so the order of the two pieces is set
a header is the top or leading part, so only the opening letter counts

parts.note: the first letter of the footballer's name
OG is the football abbreviation for an own goal

explanation.surface: A footballer named Best heads the ball and a defender called Marsh blunders into his own net.
explanation.walkthrough: George Best and Rodney Marsh were footballers, so 'Marsh' looks like a player; it is the definition. An own goal is a ball put into your own net.
explanation.definitionFit: A bog is wet, spongy ground, a straightforward synonym for a marsh or swamp.

clue.text: County rubbish tip lacking room

indicators.note: without its tip, a word loses its very first letter

parts.note: short for Bedfordshire, an English county
litter, with its first letter taken away

explanation.surface: A county council's rubbish dump has run out of space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubbish tip' looks like a dump; 'tip' is the word's first letter. Beds is the standard abbreviation for Bedfordshire.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedsitter is a single rented room used for both sleeping and living, a British term for a studio flat.

clue.text: Thunder? Goes running for something waterproof

indicators.note: running colours bleed and blur, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A storm is coming, so a camper dashes off to find rain protection.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark breaks up the fodder so it reads as a weather warning.
explanation.definitionFit: A groundsheet is a waterproof sheet laid under a tent or sleeping bag to keep out damp.

clue.text: If time is saved, more like flying for some distance

indicators.note: things flying about are scattered every which way, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Flying rather than driving saves time over a long journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'If time is saved' means T is kept in with the other letters before they are mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: A kilometre is a metric unit of length, a thousand metres, so it is one particular measured distance.

clue.text: German car wheel is sound

parts.note: a German car maker
a wheel is round like the letter O

explanation.surface: A mechanic declares that the wheel on a German car is in good condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' reads as 'in good order' but it is the noun: recorded or broadcast noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Audio refers to recorded or transmitted noise as opposed to pictures, so it means sound in the technical sense.

clue.text: One must leave sooner on quiet fishing boat

parts.note: p for piano, the musical direction to play quietly

indicators.note: whatever must leave is taken out of the word

parts.note: a synonym for sooner
the Roman numeral, the letter to be dropped

explanation.surface: Someone has to set off ahead of time on a calm day's fishing trip.
explanation.walkthrough: EARLIER loses its I and sits after P.
explanation.definitionFit: A pearler is a vessel used for diving or fishing for pearl oysters, so it is a kind of fishing craft.

clue.text: Reason for struggle with Outlook

parts.note: the point of something is the reason for it
to vie is to compete or struggle
W is a common abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: Someone explains why they are battling with their Microsoft email program.
explanation.walkthrough: Outlook is capitalised to look like the email software; it is just the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An outlook is a way of seeing things, an attitude or perspective, which is what a point of view means.

clue.text: Go west, skirting island fire

indicators.note: to skirt something is to go round its edge, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: to go west is an idiom for dying, as is to pass on
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A traveller heads west, avoiding a burning island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go west' looks like a direction; it is slang for dying.
explanation.definitionFit: Fire in the figurative sense is intense emotion or ardour, a common synonym for passion.

clue.text: I occasionally cook nosh for models

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something done occasionally happens only now and then, so only every other letter is used

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Someone sometimes makes food for catwalk models.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Models' suggests fashion models, but here it means exemplars to be imitated.
explanation.definitionFit: An icon is a revered figure held up as an example to follow, so icons are role models.

clue.text: Appalling tabloid's drawn in by spin

indicators.note: something drawn in is pulled inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a spin is a short trip out, an outing
a rag is a disparaging word for a cheap newspaper

explanation.surface: A gutter newspaper is accused of being sucked into political spin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spin' suggests media manipulation, but it is a drive out; the 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Outraging as an adjective describes something that shocks and offends deeply, the same as appalling.

clue.text: Pal spots rivals

parts.note: British informal word for a colleague or mate
spots as in places or locations

explanation.surface: A friend notices the competition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots' reads as a verb, seeing; it is the noun, places. Oppo is British slang for a friend or workmate.
explanation.definitionFit: Opposites are those set against each other, so opponents or rivals in a contest.

clue.text: Nursery crop with holes spreading

indicators.note: spreading things out scatters them, so the letters are laid down in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A garden nursery's crop is getting riddled with spreading holes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nursery' and 'crop' suggest plants; the nursery is for small children.
explanation.definitionFit: A nursery is a school for children too young for primary education, which is what a preschool is.

clue.text: Absorbed by matching notes, leaves meeting

indicators.note: something absorbed is soaked up inside, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: the same note of the sol-fa scale, te, repeated
tea leaves, the dried plant used for brewing

explanation.surface: Someone engrossed in harmonising notes walks out of a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb, departing; it is the noun, as in tea leaves. Te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale.
explanation.definitionFit: A tete-a-tete is a private conversation between two people, borrowed from French for head to head.

clue.text: Characters remaining when Hammersmith is evacuated

definitions.text: Characters remaining when Hammersmith is evacuated

parts.words: Characters remaining when Hammersmith is evacuated
parts.note: surface reading: the people left behind when a London district is cleared
setter's reading: emptying the word of its insides leaves just its first and last letters, both the same letter

explanation.walkthrough: Hammersmith is a district of west London, and 'evacuated' means emptied of its middle letters. 'Characters' are letters, not people.
explanation.definitionFit: The two letters left at either end of the place name are both the eighth letter of the alphabet, whose spelled name is the plural sought.

clue.text: Small fragment is missing lead for Lewis, TV detective

indicators.note: whatever is missing has been taken away from the word

parts.note: a morsel is a tiny piece, especially of food

indicators.note: the lead is what goes in front, so only the opening letter is meant

parts.note: the opening letter, the one to be removed

explanation.surface: A TV detective sidekick named Lewis is missing a small clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis was Inspector Morse's sergeant, and later had his own series, so the name fits the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspector Morse is the Oxford detective of novels and a long-running British television series.

clue.text: Tuneful Spice Girl tackling loud bit now and then

indicators.note: a tackler wraps round the person with the ball, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: Mel C was Sporty Spice in the pop group

indicators.note: now and then means at intervals, so only every other letter is used

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A singer from the Spice Girls is attempting a noisy passage of a song.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spice Girls had two Mels, B and C; this needs Mel C.
explanation.definitionFit: Melodic describes music with a pleasant, singable tune, so it is a direct synonym for tuneful.

clue.text: Wild fellow managed revolutionary sex clubs

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow
to run a business is to manage it

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: it is an old euphemism for sex appeal or sex
C for clubs, the card suit

explanation.surface: A wild man ran a chain of radical sex clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sex clubs' reads as one phrase, but each word gives its own letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Frantic means distraught and out of control with worry or haste, which is one sense of wild.

clue.text: Islander's bar joined by regulars from club

indicators.note: regulars are evenly spaced, so letters are taken at fixed intervals

parts.note: the first and third letters
to bar is to ban

explanation.surface: An island pub is busy with regulars from the local club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub; it means a prohibition. The 's is short for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cuban is a native of Cuba, the largest island in the Caribbean, so a particular kind of islander.

clue.text: Misty not covered by chamber musician

indicators.note: uncovered means stripped of its outer layer, so the outside letters go

parts.note: a cell is a small room
the title without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: The jazz standard Misty has not been recorded by a chamber music group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chamber' hints at chamber music, but it is a room. Misty is italicised as a song title.
explanation.definitionFit: A cellist plays the cello, so is a specific kind of musician, often found in string quartets.

clue.text: 'Hacked Off' copy has page missing

indicators.note: has something missing means that thing is taken away

parts.note: to pirate is to copy illegally
P is the abbreviation for page

explanation.surface: A copy of a book called Hacked Off is missing a page.
explanation.walkthrough: Hacked Off is styled as a title, perhaps the press-reform campaign; it is just British slang for annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: To be hacked off is British informal for being angry and fed up, which matches furious.

clue.text: Hibernian player's backside is pinched by international hard!

indicators.note: something pinched is gripped tightly between two things, so it sits inside them

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a backside is the rear end, so only the final letter is wanted

parts.note: the last letter of player
I is the abbreviation for international
H for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A Hibernian footballer gets his bottom pinched hard by an international opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: Hibernian is an Edinburgh football club, but the word also means of Ireland, from Hibernia, its Latin name.
explanation.definitionFit: Hibernia is the Latin name for Ireland, so Hibernian is a formal adjective for Irish.

clue.text: Rely on Gore to find place for donations

indicators.note: in this placing one thing sits on another and so comes after it in the word

parts.note: gore is spilt blood
to bank on is to rely on

explanation.surface: Someone counts on Al Gore to locate a charity drop-off point.
explanation.walkthrough: Gore looks like the US politician; it is blood. 'On' places one piece after the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A blood bank stores blood given by volunteer donors, so it is where those gifts are collected.

clue.text: Scans unwrapped Kipling novel

indicators.note: unwrapping removes the outer layer, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: to skim is to scan quickly

explanation.surface: A reader skims through a fresh copy of a Kipling novel.
explanation.walkthrough: SKIMS loses its outer S at each end.
explanation.definitionFit: Kim is Rudyard Kipling's 1901 novel about an orphan boy in British India.

clue.text: Heading off, get syrup

indicators.note: with the head taken off, a word loses its first letter

parts.note: to twig is British informal for to get or understand

explanation.surface: Someone leaving tells another to go and fetch golden syrup.
explanation.walkthrough: Syrup is Cockney rhyming slang: syrup of figs, wig.
explanation.definitionFit: In rhyming slang syrup of figs stands for wig, shortened to its first word as usual.

clue.text: Cleans grime off dairy product

indicators.note: something gone off has spoiled and changed, so the letters go wrong

parts.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone scrubs dirt from a dairy product.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off' sits naturally after 'grime', and also hints at milk going sour.
explanation.definitionFit: Single cream is a thin pouring cream, lower in fat than double, sold in British shops.
